1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run time
2	
3	**count stage**
4	: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library and prints its errors: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count. Where an early stage of the checker finds errors in an api or a component, the checker skips its overloading and return-type checks there. So the count misses the errors of those checks there, and a fix of an early error can raise it.
5	
6	The code of this area is in these directories:
7	
8	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
9	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
10	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
11	
12	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.
13	
14	## What the two paths share
15	
16	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
17	
18	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
19	- Number natives: walk's `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`), and the compiled `nativeHelpers/` (`simpleIntArith.java`).
20	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
21	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
22	
23	The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.
24	
25	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
26	
27	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
28	
29	Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay.
30	
31	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
32	
33	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
34	
35	- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
36	- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
37	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
38	
39	It also refuses a function, method, object or trait declaration with a `where` clause of its own, and a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose `extends` entry has a `where` clause. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private` and `abstract`, such as `override` (ledger row 650).
40	
41	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
42	
43	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
44	
45	## What the code generator does
46	
47	`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time", gives the jars, the dispatch methods, the templates and the boxed numbers.
48	
49	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
50	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
51	- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
52	- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet (`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time"). If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):
53	
54	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'
55	
56	## The run time
57	
58	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
59	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.
60	
61	## Natives
62	
63	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
64	
65	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.
66	
67	## Traps of the compiled path
68	
69	- Before disambiguation, the compiled path bounds an unbounded type parameter by `Object`, not `Any`. Walk does not. So the compiled path rejects every generic that is instantiated at a tuple type, until the switch-over (ledger row 412).
70	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
71	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
72	
73	## The checker's gaps
74	
75	`revival-changes.md` gives the rules. This section gives where the checker applies them, and where it does not yet.
76	
77	- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786). It accepts `g[\T\](a: T)` beside `g(a: Any)`, whose declared domains are equal, and runs the generic one (ledger row 759).
78	- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the code generator refuses such a declaration (ledger row 701). A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
79	  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
80	  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
81	  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
82	- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
83	- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).
84

86	
87	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
88	
89	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
90	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
91	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.

97	    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)

133	## The checker's time
134	
135	This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
136	
137	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 seconds, more under load. It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
138	
139	The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:
140	
141	- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
142	- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.
143	
144	A node's hash starts from its class's name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks or a union's members, moves only where the change itself moves it. Such a move is a difference: keep the old order, or report the difference, as for any other.
145	
146	`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node, so one long walker method slows the whole checker. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.
147	
148	The timing is a smoke test. It is there to catch a slowdown of several times, or of orders of magnitude: a change that makes the checker three times slower must show. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.
149	
150	If you change the checker:
151	
152	1. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
153	2. Time the base build and the change, named `base` and `change`. Run the base in a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), and the change in a call set up for your tree, each in the background (`session.md`). Use the same command for both, with `N` the run's name:
154	
155	       export W=<your tree> N=base ; mkdir -p $W/tmp/count
156	       time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$N.txt $W/tmp/count/$N
157	
158	3. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
159	4. After the second pass, run the count stage once more with the command of step 2, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite").
160	5. If the pass reuses an answer that the checker computed earlier, as a memo does, audit it on one full run. Put the audit in an instrumented copy ("Testing an edit here"), never in the tree. In the audit, compute each reused answer again and compare the two. If any answer differs, the reuse is wrong: fix it or drop it, then repeat step 4. Report the count of reuses and of differences.
161	6. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, the comparison of their `run.txt` files, and that `pass` has the same results as `change`.
162	
163	To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and the methods over 8,000 bytes that `MethodSizeJUTest` lists in its source. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):
164	
165	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings' 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings'
166	
167	If your brief asks you to review a change of the checker, run the count stage yourself. Time the base build and the worker's commit of step 1 once each, as step 2 says, with the commit and the worker's head in worktrees seeded at them (`worktrees.md`). Check that your times are the worker's, in order of size. Check that the commit's and the head's results are the same.

1	# Writing a test
2	
3	**gated test**
4	: Test that the gate's suites run.
5	
6	**green**
7	: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as passed.
8	
9	**red**
10	: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as failed.
11	
12	**`XXX` test**
13	: Gated expected failure. It asserts the answer that the specification gives, and fails today. The harness reports it green while it fails, and red when the defect is fixed.
14	
15	## A test program
16	
17	A test program has this form:
18	
19	    component Name
20	    export Executable
21	
22	    (* declarations *)
23	
24	    run(): () = do
25	        assert(f(2), 4, "f(2)")
26	    end
27	
28	    end
29	
30	- `(*)` starts a comment to the end of the line. It cannot hold `*)`: the parser ends the comment there and refuses the program. `(* ... *)` comments nest.
31	- A compiled test with a `run` key ends `run()` with `println("PASS")`, unless a `run_out` key checks its output (below).
32	- Under walk, `assert(x, y, msg)` checks that `x` equals `y`. It and `=/=` call a type's own `=` only if the type extends a `FortressLibrary` trait that declares `=`, such as `Equality`. Otherwise they compare by identity (ledger row 807). If a type `P` has its own `=`, make `P` extend `Equality[\P\]`, or write `assert(x = y, msg)`. The compiler's library declares the two-value `assert` only for `ZZ32`, `String` and `Character`; its `assert(flag, msg)` takes any `Boolean`.
33	- Do not name a variable or a parameter after a functional method of the library, such as `big`, `even`, `numerator` or `shift`. The disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses it: "Variable even is already declared."
34	- Under walk, a numeral does not bind to `NN32` or `NN64`, and a numeral with a radix point does not bind to `RR32` (ledger row 454). Write `a: NN32 = unsigned(5)`, not `a: NN32 = 5`.
35	
36	## Where a test goes, and how it passes
37	
38	Interpreter (walk): write `ProjectFortress/tests/Name.fss`, whose component is `Name`.
39	
40	- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
41	- It is green if it throws no exception, exits 0, and neither its standard output nor its standard error contains `fail` or `FAIL`. A longer word counts too: `failure` fails the test. Only a file whose name contains `QuickCheckTest` is exempt.
42	- An api that it imports, and a helper component, go in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`. In `tests/`, a helper would run as a test.
43	- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
44	- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test with such a `.test` file is green if the program loads and runs clean.
45	
46	Compiled: write `Name.fss` and `Name.test` in the compiled test folder that holds tests of its kind:
47	
48	- `library_tests/`: the compiler's library. A test of the interpreter's library is an interpreter test (above).
49	- `parser_tests/`: the parser.
50	- `compiler_tests/`: the rest, beside the team's numbered `CompiledN` tests.
51	- `other_compiler_tests/`: the team's compiled tests that do not fit the `CompiledN` series, by the comment in `OtherCompilerJUTest.java`. Put no new test there.
52	
53	The `.test` files are the whole list of tests: a `.fss` that no `.test` file names never runs. A `.test` file is a Java property file. It names the commands to run and the checks on their output, as lit's RUN and CHECK lines do:
54	
55	    tests=Name                 the component(s) it drives; without it, the .test file's own name
56	    compile | link | typecheck each present command is one JUnit case; link compiles, then links
57	    run                        run the linked program in a subprocess (bin/fortress run)
58	    <command>_<stream>_<check>=text
59	                               command: compile, link or run; stream: out, err or exception;
60	                               check: contains, does_not_contain, equals, matches,
61	                               WIcontains (containment with runs of whitespace collapsed)
62	
63	A `run` fails if the program exits non-zero or a `run_*` check fails. With no `run_out` check, its output must contain `pass` or `PASS`. For example:
64	
65	    tests=EqualityRung1
66	    link
67	    run
68	    run_out_WIcontains=PASS

71	
72	- Under walk, an `XXX` test is `tests/XXXName.fss`, whose component is `XXXName`. With no `.test` file, it is green when it fails as a plain test would.
73	- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name applies to every command that the file drives: each must fail. So a defect at run time, whose link succeeds, needs two `.test` files ("Writing an `XXX` test").
74	- An unmet `run_*` check makes a run test red, whatever the prefix.
75	- The harness reports any link or compile exception of a component whose name contains `XXX` as expected, whatever the `.test` file's name. Only an unmet key of that command makes it red.
76	- An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key, whose program compiles, reports "Saw wrong failure", which is red.
77	- A green `XXX` test prints `Saw expected failure` or `OK Saw expected exception`.

80	
81	Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:
82	
83	1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
84	2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
85	3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, or no gated test can pass while it shows, as when walk crashes on the program, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.

If your tree already holds the fix, run the test through the harness on the old code, as `worktrees.md`, "Running the old code", says.

In an edit of the original tree, put every check into a gated test, never into a one-off script. A probe that only measures may use its own script. 1	# Running tests
2	
3	**track**
4	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.
5	
6	**shard**
7	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.
8	
9	**code state**
10	: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.
11	
12	## The two suites
13	
14	`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:
15	
16	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
17	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
18	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
19	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.
20	
21	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.
22	
23	`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
24	
25	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
26	
27	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
28	
29	The two suites work in the same way:
30	
31	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
32	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
33	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
34	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
35	
36	To run a suite:
37	
38	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
39	- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
40	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
41	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
42	
43	## The switches that the harness reads
44	
45	Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.
46	
47	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
48	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
49	- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
50	- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
51	- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
52	- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.
53	
54	## Outside the gate
55	
56	- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
57	- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).
58	
59	## When to run a whole suite
60	
61	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
62	- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk or of a phase that both paths share, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
63	  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
64	  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
65	  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`) or the parser, run both.
66	- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
67	- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
68	- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the run time (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
69	- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.
70	
71	The suites do not check these:
72	
73	- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
74	- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
75	- the linker's aliasing of apis;
76	- `fortress unparse`;
77	- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
78	- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.
79	
80	If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.
81	
82	## One test, or a few
83	
84	Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.
85	
86	### Interpreter tests
87	
88	Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:
89	
90	    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
91	        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]
92	
93	- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
94	- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
95	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
96	- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
97	- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
98	- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
99	- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.
100	
101	To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:
102	
103	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss
104	
105	The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").
106	
107	### Compiled tests
108	
109	Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).
110	
111	The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.
112	
113	    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
114	        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1
115	
116	- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
117	- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
118	- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
119	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
120	- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
121	- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.
122	
123	To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:
124	
125	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test
126	
127	Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

129	## One unit-test class, or one track

131	To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.
132	
133	To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:

135	- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.

8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.

24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.

34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it.

38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:

1	# The library
2	
3	The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
4	
5	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
6	- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
7	- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
8	- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.
9	
10	## How loops and reductions call the library
11	
12	The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:
13	
14	- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
15	- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
16	- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.
17	
18	These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.
19	
20	## The curator's decisions on the library
21	
22	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
23	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
24	- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
25	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
26	- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
27	- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.
28	
29	## Designing a change
30	
31	- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
32	- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
33	- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
34	- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
35	- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
36	- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
37	- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
38	- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
39	- A new native is a Java class under `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"), so it is an edit of walk's Java too.
40	- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.
41	
42	## Editing
43	
44	A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.
45

1	# The specification
2	
3	Three folders hold the team's specification:
4	
5	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
6	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
7	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
8	
9	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
10	
11	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
12	
13	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
14	
15	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
16	
17	## Changing the text: the revision form
18	
19	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
20	
21	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
22	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
23	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
24	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
25	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
26	
27	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
28	
29	2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
30	
31	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
32	
33	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.
34	
35	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
36	
37	4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
38	
39	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
40	
41	Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.
42	
43	## Building it
44	
45	To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
46	
47	    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
48	
49	- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'Reference .* undefined\|multiply defined\|Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
50	- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
51	- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
52	- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.
53	
54	## When the text and an implementation disagree
55	
56	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
57	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
58	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.
59	
60	## Citing it
61	
62	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
63	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.
64

# Rung E of climb batch 21b: the api aligned with its component, and the export check brought to its rule

- problem: the export error of the last landed gate, one site whose message names 43 traits and objects of `FortressLibrary` (`explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv:2`), and the export probe that sorted them into 115 differences and found the check's three defects, rows 800 to 802 (`explorations/perf-probes/export-check-full/REPORT.md:5-25`, `:304-329`).
- spec: `Specification/basic/components/apis.tex:250-257` ("A matching definition of a declaration $d$ is a definition $d'$ with the same name as $d$ that includes definitions for all declarations other than the methods or fields declared abstract in $d$"), with `Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:372-385`.
- precedent: the check's own `equalIdOrOps` for names (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/ExportChecker.scala:560-568`); the probe's shadow for 4i (`explorations/perf-probes/export-check-full/export-check-shadow.patch`, its `isAbstractMember` and count rule); the api's own `abstract` members for the 4h lines (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1578`); `close` and `whenUnconsumed` beside `consume` for the prelude's line (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:1168-1169`).
- deviation: the message of a field names it, "different field x @", where the check said "different field @" (`ExportChecker.scala:799-803`); a field needs no definition only when every name it declares is abstract, where the shadow took any (`ExportChecker.scala:775-779`); one line of the compiler's prelude, outside the files the brief names (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:1170`).
- historical: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/ExportChecker.scala`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`.

## 1. What changed and why

Two commits on `wip/rung-export-align`, from the base `aa5c67d48`, both pushed:

- `687c4dcfa`: five compiled tests, each an api and its component, seen failing on the base (section 2).
- `18179f051`: the check, the api, one prelude line, one test respelled and one expected failure added.

**The check** (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/ExportChecker.scala`):

- Row 800: `equalFnHeaders` compares the two declarations' names, through a new `equalNames` that hands two `IdOrOp`s to the check's own `equalIdOrOps` (api, text, fixity, enclosing) (`:597-604`, called at `:612`). `equalMember` and `existsMatching` both go through it, so a trait's member is matched by its name and its header; a top-level function's two sides already share the name, from `matchFirst`.
- Row 801: `equalLValue`'s comparison of names and modifiers is joined to its type match in one expression (`:841-845`). Before, Scala ended the statement at the newline before `(`, and the type match alone was the result.
- Row 802: `allAbstractsMadePublic` calls `equalMember(r, d)`, the api's member first, as `equalMember` takes them (`:761`).
- 4i: `isAbstractMember` (`:775-779`); `equalListMembers` counts the api's members that are not abstract against the component's (`:791`), and an api member written `abstract` needs no matching member (`:796`). The method's comment quotes `apis.tex` (`:783-787`).
- The field's message names the field (`:799-803`), as a method's names the method.

**The api** (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`): the planner's `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-21/probes/run2-api.patch`, applied with `git apply` as it is: 88 declaration lines, 87 insertions and 64 deletions (section 6 lists them).

**The prelude** (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:1170`): `consume(): () throws IOException`, as its api declares it (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:600`) and as its siblings `close` and `whenUnconsumed` write it on both sides (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:1168-1169`); the native it calls throws as theirs do (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/fileOps.java:65-75`). The name check refused the prelude without it (section 3); by reading, the stock check had matched the api's `consume` through `close` or `whenUnconsumed`, whose header `(): () throws IOException` is the same. Nothing calls `consume` in the compiled path (grep of `CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/Compiler*.fss` and the three compiled test folders).

**The tests** (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/`):

| Test | Shape | Base | Now |
|---|---|---|---|
| `XXXExportMemberName` | api `trait T f(): ZZ32 end`, component `trait T g(): ZZ32 = 1 end` | compiles (rc 0) | refused, `compile_err_contains=different method f` |
| `XXXExportFieldName` | api `object O x: ZZ32 end`, component `object O var y: ZZ32 := 1 end` | compiles (rc 0) | refused, `different field x` |
| `ExportComprisesEllipsisAbstract` | api `trait Q comprises { ... } abstract num(self): ZZ32 end`, component `trait Q comprises { R }` with the same member and `object R extends Q` defining it; `num(q)` with `q: Q = R` | refused, 'Asbtract method num ... is not declared in the API' | links, runs, `PASS` |
| `ExportAbstractMemberDefined` | api `abstract f(): ZZ32`, component `f(): ZZ32 = 1` | refused, 'different method f' | compiles |
| `ExportAbstractMemberAbsent` | api `abstract f(): ZZ32` and `g(): ZZ32`, component `g(): ZZ32 = 2` only | refused, 'missing members of the trait/object in the component' | compiles |
| `XXXFunctionalMethodComprisedObject`, with `FunctionalMethodComprisedObjectLink` | `num(R)` on the object itself, the same trait and object without an api | links; the run dies, `NoSuchMethodError` | the same, an expected failure (section 8, NEW-E-1) |

`ExportComprisesEllipsisAbstract` first called `num(R)`, which the compiled path cannot run whatever the export check does (section 8). == Specification/basic/components/apis.tex:181-272

\section{Component and API Identity}

Formally, we introduce two functions on components,
$\imports$ and $\exports$,
that return the imported and exported \apisN\ of the component, respectively.
For any component $\comp$, %% \in \components$,
$\imports(\comp) \intersect \exports(\comp) = \emptyset$.
This restriction is required throughout to ground the semantics of
operations on components, as discussed in \secref{basicops}.

Every component
has a unique name, used for the purposes of component linking.
This name includes a user-provided identifier.
In the case of a simple component, the identifier is determined by
a component name given at
the top of the source file from which it is compiled.
A build script may keep a tally on version numbers and append them to the
first line of a component,
incrementing its tally on each compilation.
The name of a compound component is specified as an argument
to the \shellcommand{link} operation (described in \secref{basicops})
that defines it.
Component equivalence is determined nominally
to allow mutually recursive linking of components.
By programmer convention, identifiers associated with components
that are not included in \library\
begin with the reverse of the URL of the development team.
%Two components with the same name must be identical, even if they are
%contained in different fortresses.
A fortress does not allow the installation of
distinct components with the same name.
Component names are used during
\shellcommand{link} and \shellcommand{upgrade}
operations to ensure that the restrictions on
upgrades to a component are respected,
as explained in \secref{basicops}.

Every component also includes
a vendor name,
the name of the fortress it is compiled on, and
a timestamp, denoting the time of compilation.
The time of compilation is measured by the compiling fortress,
and the name of the fortress is provided by the fortress automatically.
Every timestamp issued by a fortress must be unique.
The vendor name typically remains the same throughout a significant
portion of the life of a
user account, and is best provided as a user environment variable.

Every \apiN\ has a unique name that consists of a user-provided identifier.
As with components,
\apiN\ equivalence is determined nominally.
Every \apiN\ also includes a vendor name,
the name of the fortress it is compiled on,
and a timestamp.
\note{
Victor: Is it the \apiN\ name that includes the vendor, etc.?
It used to just say \apiN, and I changed it to \apiN\ name.

Jan: I changed it back, because we don't claim to distinguish APIs
  this way in the remainder of the text, and don't give a
  mechanism for specifying these details in an import.}
Component names must not conflict with \apiN\ names.
For convenience, a compiler can also
produce an \apiN\ directly from a project
with the same name as the component it is derived from.
Such an \apiN\ includes \emph{matching} declarations of the component.
All declarations in the component appear in the API.


A component must include, for every \apiN\ $A$ it exports,
matching definitions for all the declarations in $A$.
A matching definition of a declaration $d$
is a definition $d'$ with the same name as $d$
that includes definitions for all declarations
other than the methods or fields declared \KWD{abstract} in $d$.
The header and type of $d'$ must be the same as the header and type of $d$.
$d'$ may include additional definitions not declared in $d$.

Other than its identity,
the only relevant characteristic of an \apiN\ $\api$
is the set of \apisN\ that it uses,
denoted by $\uses(\api)$.
Because an \apiN\ $\api$ might expose types
defined in $\uses(\api)$,
we require that a component that exports $\api$
also exports all \apisN\ in $\uses(\api)$ that it does not import.
Formally, the following condition holds on the exported \apisN\
of a component $\comp$:
\[
\api \in \exports(\comp) \logicand \api' \in \uses(\api)
        \implies \api' \in \imports(\comp) \union \exports(\comp)
\]

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table holds a total; 1 if no table could be produced, or if the table holds
# no total because the run's errors are not the checker's (#stopped, below). 20 s in the
# main tree, measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from
# explorations/perf-probes/prelude/, so that the gate does not depend on a probe
# directory: WorldFlip.java (Shell.useInterpreterLibraries() plus
# PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder, both public, which is the world switch without an edit
# to a tracked file) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
# perf-probes/prelude/run-all.sh:33-35. A copy of a tracked source goes stale silently,
# so the checksum of the tracked one is recorded here and the table's "#shadow" line
# says whether it still matches.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false, read
# at OverloadingChecker.scala:77), since 2026-09-27 (climb batch 7). The memo is keyed on
# declaration pairs and hides 27 to 35 errors depending on the build order once an api's
# overloading check runs (perf-probes/nat/triage.md section 1; FACTS.md, "The hidden
# layer, classified"); with it off every build gives one count. The table's "#cache"

\emph{AbsFldDecl}
&::=& \option{\emph{AbsFldMods}} \emph{AbsFldWTypes}\\

\emph{ApiFldMod} &::=& \KWD{hidden} $|$ \KWD{settable} $|$ \KWD{test}\\

\end{Grammar}


Traits may also include abstract field declarations that are implicit
declarations of abstract getter methods.
Syntactically, an abstract field declaration consists of an optional
sequence of modifiers followed by the field name, followed by the token
`\EXP{\COLONOP}', and the type of the field.


By default, a field declaration implicitly
declares a getter method for the field unless there is an explicit
getter declared in the enclosing trait.
An implicit getter method takes no arguments, has the same name as the
field, and has a return type equal to the field type.  When called, the
implicit getter returns the value of the field when called.




Abstract field declarations can include the following special modifiers:
\paragraph{\KWD{hidden}:}
A field declaration with the
modifier \KWD{hidden} has no implicit getter method.


\paragraph{\KWD{settable}:}
A field declaration with the modifier \KWD{settable} has an implicit
setter method unless there is an explicit setter declared in the enclosing
trait.  An implicit setter method takes a parameter
(with no default expression) whose type is the type of the field, and
returns \EXP{()}. When called, the implicit setter rebinds the
corresponding field to its argument.
If a field declaration includes the modifier  \KWD{settable} and
\KWD{hidden}, only an abstract setter is declared.
%
If a field declaration includes the modifier \KWD{hidden} without
\KWD{settable}, it is a static error.
If an abstract field declaration includes the modifier \KWD{settable},
it is mutable.
Because the \KWD{settable} modifier implies \KWD{var}, and
the \KWD{var} modifier without \KWD{settable} only affects implementations,
abstract field declarations do not include the \KWD{var} modifier.




\paragraph{\KWD{wrapped}:}
If a field declaration of $f$ has the modifier \KWD{wrapped}
and the type of $f$ is trait type $T$, and $T$ is not a naked type variable,
then the enclosing trait $S$ implicitly includes ``forwarding methods'' for
all methods in $T$ that are also inherited from any supertrait of $S$.
Each of these methods simply calls
the corresponding method on the trait referred to by field $f$.
